# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Data missingness shows up in many real-life scenarios, arising from different sources like improper data collection, malfunctioning equipment, or operational data loss. In all these scenarios, imputation, which is the process of filling data gaps with estimated values, is a widely accepted approach to complete missing data for machine learning and deep-learning tasks such as classification and regression. For instance, biomedical data frequently suffers from extensive missingness due to patient behavior, poor data management, and biased sampling, which complicates downstream analyses like patient stratification.<!-- imputation is the process of replacing values with estimated values, make connection between missiing data in real life and known techniques in ML. Be more explicit about what kind of downstream task -->

However, it is well-known that all types of imputation induce biases in the data that can negatively impact the downstream task, and recent work has shown that improvements in the quality of imputation do not necessarily result in improvement in downstream task performance. In particular, the quality of imputation decreases when the size of the dataset is small. In this thesis, I will focus on datasets with small sample sizes, which for example arise very often in real-world scenarios. Small datasets can in particular reduce the quality of simple imputation due to sampling error, especially in the case of heterogeneous features.

In this thesis, I will explore techniques to incorporate the objective of downstream tasks explicitly into learning with missing data. For this, I first look at \acr{kNN} imputation on tabular data. Secondly, I look into short time series data with regular structural missingness. Finally I look at missingness in graph-structured data. First I argue that nearest neighbor-based imputation methods can outperform advanced deep neural network-based and generative approaches. In particular, I derive theoretical guarantees for the quality of \acr{kNN} imputation under different missingness scenarios. I then introduce \acr{F3I} as a modification of the \acr{kNN} approach with a novel loss function, that nevertheless preserves those same theoretical guarantees. Furthermore, I show that jointly training a hyperparameter-tunable loss function that forms a homotopy between the imputation and downstream objectives can further improve downstream task performance, thereby going beyond the conventional impute-then-classify paradigm. Secondly, I consider settings where the missingness is structurally regular, such as in short multivariate time series with missing time points or missing features. For these problems, I develop \acr{MUDRA} to show that discretization-invariant feature extraction and classification based on functional data analysis techniques can outperform the classical impute-then-extract features paradigm. Finally, I consider missing labels in more complex structured data, such as graph-structured datasets. I then develop a method called \acr{FUSE} to show how the inherent local and global community structures of the network can be used to construct informative node features for imputing the missing labels, in a more accurate and computationally efficient manner than random walk or mutual information-based formulations.
<!--Mention each method you developed-->

These results demonstrate that imputation quality alone should not be the sole criterion for evaluating and constructing missing-data methods for real-life applications. Since imputation is ultimately performed to facilitate downstream analysis, the objectives of the downstream task should be explicitly incorporated into the design and evaluation of learning algorithms on missing data. This can be achieved either by jointly optimizing imputation and downstream objectives, as in the proposed loss-based \acr{F3I} approach, or by bypassing imputation altogether when the structure of the data permits, as in the functional data analysis-based approach \acr{MUDRA}. More broadly, this thesis advocates for a task-oriented perspective on missing data, in which the success of an imputation method is ultimately determined not only by how accurately it reconstructs missing values, but also by how effectively it supports the downstream task.
